Welcome to the 2026 Connectomics Research Competition (Connectome2026).

The brain is one of the most complex systems known in nature. To understand how it works, neuroscientists investigate the brain across multiple levels of analysis—from individual neurons and synapses, to neural circuits, to large-scale networks spanning the entire brain.

A central goal of neuroscience is to understand how the brain’s physical structure gives rise to its function. How does a seemingly fixed network of neurons and connections produce dynamic patterns of activity? How do these patterns of activity support perception, learning, memory, decision-making, and consciousness? How do changes in brain organization contribute to neurological and psychiatric disorders?

At the heart of these questions lies the field of connectomics: the study of the brain’s wiring and organizational principles. Connectomics seeks to map and understand both the structural connections that physically link neurons and brain regions, and the functional connections that emerge when different parts of the brain coordinate their activity.

In Connectome2026, you will work with real scientific datasets and modern research tools to explore these questions firsthand. You will analyze the cutting-edge datasets used by researchers around the world and investigate open questions about how brains are organized and how they function.
To help participants explore connectomics across multiple scales, the competition is organized into two complementary tracks.

In this track, you will investigate the structural connectome of the adult Drosophila melanogaster (fruit fly) brain.

Using one of the most detailed brain maps ever created, you will explore how individual neurons are connected through millions of synaptic connections. Participants will learn how to visualize neurons, trace neural pathways, analyze connectivity patterns, and develop hypotheses about how neural circuits process information and give rise to cognition.

This track focuses primarily on microscale connectomics and the structural organization of neural circuits underlying behaviour.

In this track, you will investigate the human functional connectome using large-scale neuroimaging data collected from over 200 participants.

You will explore how different brain regions coordinate their activity, construct and analyze functional brain networks, and investigate how patterns of functional connectivity relate to cognition, behavior, and individual differences across people.

This track focuses primarily on macroscale connectomics and the functional organization of the human brain.

Each track contains two levels of difficulty: Introductory and Advanced. Both levels provide substantial guidance, learning resources, and access to the same core datasets and analysis tools. The primary difference lies in the depth of analysis and the degree of independent research expected.

The Introductory Level is designed to help participants develop foundational skills in neuroscience research, data analysis, and scientific thinking.

Participants will learn how to use the datasets and tools provided in the competition, perform guided analyses, interpret their findings, and gain familiarity with the types of questions neuroscientists ask when studying the brain. This level emphasizes building confidence with connectomics concepts, research workflows, and scientific communication.

The Advanced Level is designed for participants who wish to pursue more in-depth and open-ended investigations.

While using many of the same datasets and tools as the Introductory Level, participants are encouraged to formulate their own research questions (with guidance), perform deeper analyses, explore additional methodologies, and develop novel insights from the data. This level places greater emphasis on independent scientific inquiry and creativity.

Participants are welcome to choose the level that best matches their interests, goals, and experience.
Participants may engage with the competition in different ways depending on their goals.

To receive a participation certificate, participants must successfully complete and submit work for any track at any level.

Whether you choose to explore fly connectomics, human connectomics, or both, we encourage you to focus on your learning, exploration, and scientific curiosity.

To be considered for competition awards and cash prizes, participants must:

Complete both competition tracks:

Synapse-Level Connectomics (Flies)

Macroscale Connectomics (Humans)

AND complete at least one track at the Advanced Level.

This structure encourages participants to develop an appreciation for neuroscience across multiple scales while providing opportunities for deeper, more independent research.

Neuroscientists study the brain across multiple levels, from individual neurons and synapses to whole-brain networks.

A major goal of neuroscience is to understand how brain structure gives rise to brain function, cognition, and behavior.

Connectomics is the study of the brain’s structural and functional organization.

Track 1 focuses on microscale connectomics using the synapse-level wiring diagram of the Drosophila brain.

Track 2 focuses on macroscale connectomics using human functional neuroimaging data from over 200 participants.

Each track contains both Introductory and Advanced levels.

To receive a participation certificate, participants may complete at least one track at any level.

To be eligible for awards and cash prizes, participants must complete both tracks and complete at least one track at the Advanced Level.
The 2026 Connectomics Research Competition is open to students worldwide and features two prize categories.

This category is intended for students who, on July 1, 2026, are:

Currently enrolled in high school; or

Taking a gap year after completing high school; and

Have not yet begun post-secondary studies (e.g., college, university, or equivalent).

This category is intended for students who, on July 1, 2026, are:

Currently enrolled in a post-secondary institution (e.g., college or university); and

Have not yet completed their first undergraduate degree.

Students enrolled in undergraduate-entry professional programs (e.g., MBBS or equivalent programs entered directly from high school) are eligible to participate in the Undergraduate Category.

However, participants who have already completed an undergraduate degree before July 1, 2026—including those enrolled in graduate-entry medicine, graduate-entry law, master’s programs, PhD programs, or other postgraduate programs—are not eligible for undergraduate prizes.

Everyone, regardless of their age and educational level, is welcome to use our resource and submit for participation certificates!

Working individually ensures that every participant has the opportunity to engage directly with the data, develop their own ideas, and take ownership of their learning journey.

Yes.

As long as you have not started your post-secondary education before July 1, 2026, you remain eligible for the High School Category.

This includes students who have completed their high school examinations, graduated from high school, or are currently taking a gap year before beginning university.

records.content:
You are welcome to participate in the competition, but you will not be eligible for undergraduate awards or prizes.

If you completed your final undergraduate course requirements and effectively finished your first undergraduate degree before July 1, 2026, you are considered to have completed your undergraduate studies for the purpose of prize eligibility, regardless of your official graduation or convocation date.

However, if you are on a summer break and have not yet completed all degree requirements—for example, if you still need to complete future coursework in order to graduate—you remain eligible for the Undergraduate Category.

This reflects the fact that many universities worldwide view pre-university CEGEP as a transitional stage between secondary and undergraduate education, and completion of the program is generally required before beginning undergraduate studies.

Submissions will be evaluated based on the quality of the participant’s engagement with the competition, the strength of their scientific reasoning, the clarity of their communication, and the extent to which they make effective use of the provided datasets and tools.

Because Connectome2026 is a learning-focused research competition, judges will value:

Genuine engagement with the data and tools

Clear scientific thinking and reasoning

Appropriate use of evidence, figures, and citations

Originality, curiosity, and initiative

Effective communication to the intended audience

Participants will not be evaluated solely on the strength, novelty, or statistical significance of their findings. In many cases, unexpected, inconclusive, or null results can be just as scientifically valuable as positive findings.

Instead, judges will place greater emphasis on whether the analyses are appropriate and well-executed, whether conclusions are supported by the evidence and relevant scientific literature, and whether participants demonstrate thoughtful interpretation and meaningful engagement with the dataset.

For participants being considered for awards and cash prizes, judges will evaluate both the written reports and video submissions.

The overall score will be weighted as follows:

Written Reports: 60%

Video Submission(s): 40%

Because participants submit work from two competition tracks, the written report component will be weighted according to the depth of work completed:

80% from the report corresponding to your Advanced-Level track (or, if both tracks are completed at the advanced level, the stronger of the two reports)

20% from the report corresponding to the other track

This weighting reflects the greater depth of analysis, independence, and scientific inquiry expected in Advanced-Level submissions while still recognizing engagement across both competition tracks.

The video component will be assessed based on your strongest video submission.

Participants who submit separate videos for each track will be evaluated using the stronger of the two videos. Participants who submit a single combined video covering both tracks will be evaluated based on that submission.

This approach allows participants flexibility in how they communicate their work while ensuring that all participants are assessed on their ability to communicate scientific ideas clearly and effectively to a broader audience.

The report identifies a clear question or aim and provides a reasonable explanation for why it matters.
The report indicates an overall topic or direction, but the rationale is somewhat general or underdeveloped.
The report lacks a clear question, purpose, or rationale.

This page explains the deliverables required for conn2026 and how to submit them.

For the competition, you will be submitting two types of deliverables:

Video submission via Clematis Discord

Written report via Google Form

The two deliverables serve different purposes:

Video submission: intended for a general audience, including people who are not neuroscientists. This is your opportunity to communicate your research journey, key ideas, and/or main findings in an accessible and engaging way.

Written report: a more formal research report written for a neuroscience audience.
The number of deliverables depends on how many tracks you choose to submit.

You must submit:

one video submission via Discord, reflecting on your journey and findings for your chosen track

one written report via Google Form for your chosen track

You must submit:

Video submission via Discord: either

one combined video covering both tracks, or

two separate videos, one for each track

Written report via Google Form: 2 separate written reports, one for each track

If you are participating for a participation certificate, you may submit work for one track.

If you are aiming to be considered for awards, you must submit work for both tracks, and at least one track must be at the Advanced Level.

All video submissions must be posted in #conn2026 on the Clematis Discord server: 

https://​tinyurl​.com​/discordclematis

The video submission is intended for a general audience, including your fellow participants and the broader Clematis community of over 1,000 learners from around the world. This is an opportunity to communicate your research journey, discoveries, challenges, and insights in an accessible and engaging way.

Unlike the written report, which is intended for a neuroscience audience, the video submission encourages you to share your work with people from a wide range of backgrounds and levels of expertise.

There is no required format for the video, but the video should be no longer than 10 minutes. We encourage participants to be creative and choose a style that best communicates their work. Examples include:

Short-form videos (e.g., TikTok, Instagram Reel, YouTube Short)

Long-form videos (e.g., videos with slides)

Animated videos

Screen recordings demonstrating analyses or visualizations

Research journey or reflection videos

Any other creative audiovisual format that effectively communicates your work

The focus is not on professional video production, but on clearly and effectively sharing your experience and/or findings.

Submission must include a video.

You are not required to show your face in the video, although you are welcome to do so if you wish.

If your video contains narration or spoken commentary, the voice must be your own voice.

Generative AI voiceovers, synthetic narration, or text-to-speech voices are not permitted.

Other uses of generative AI remain subject to the competition’s Generative AI policy.

Participants are encouraged to include a short text caption in their Discord post describing their project, research question, findings, or learning experience.

You may upload your video directly to Discord or share a link to a video hosted on another platform, including YouTube, Google Drive, OneDrive, Dropbox, social media platforms (e.g., Instagram, Facebook, and LinkedIn).

As long as the video is accessible to judges and organizers, participants may choose the hosting platform that works best for them.

Writing a Guided Research Commentary (Introductory Level)

records.content: For the introductory level, you will be developing foundational skills in neuroscience research. Based on our guided exercise, you will write a research commentary of 500-1000 words summarizing your analyses, observations, and interpretations.

Writing a scientific report may feel unfamiliar if this is your first research project. Fortunately, many of the skills used by professional researchers can be learned through practice and guidance.

For the Advanced Level of both competition tracks, your written report will take the form of a research manuscript. We encourage you to communicate your research in a format similar to that used by scientists when sharing their work with the broader research community in a peer-reviewed journal.

Below is a concise guide to writing a research paper produced by the Taylor & Francis Group (2021), one of the world’s largest academic publishing companies. The guide provides practical advice on structuring a scientific manuscript, as well as tips for communicating research clearly and effectively. For the competition, your written report will include an introduction, methods, results, discussion, conclusion, and abstract, and title.

If the image does not display correctly, you can


open it directly here.

Source

Taylor & Francis Group. (2021). Writing your paper: Everything you need to know to prepare and write an effective research paper. 

https://​authorservices​.taylorandfrancis​.com​/wp​-content​/uploads​/2021​/03​/Writing​_your​_paper​_ebook​.pdf

The expected word count varies depending on the level of submission:

Introductory Level: approximately 500–1,000 words

Advanced Level: approximately 2,000–4,000 words

These ranges are intended as guidelines. There is no formal word limit for either level. However, scientific communication is most effective when it is concise and focused. We therefore recommend that participants do not exceed 7,000 words, unless there is a compelling reason to do so.

If you need to write an abstract (i.e., for advanced level submissions) we recommend that the abstract be no longer than 350 words.

There are no strict formatting requirements for written reports submitted to Connectome2026.

Participants are welcome to use any formatting style, provided that the report is clear, readable, well-organized, and consistent throughout.

That said, if you are unsure where to begin, the following conventions are commonly used in academic writing:

Font: Times New Roman, Arial, or Calibri.

Font size: 11–12 pt

Line spacing: 1.5 or double-spaced

Page margins: approximately 1 inch (2.54 cm) on all sides

Page numbering: recommended for longer reports

Section headings: clearly labelled and used consistently

For Advanced-Level submissions, we additionally recommend including clear section headings such as:

Abstract

Introduction

Methods

Results

Discussion

References

Ultimately, judges will evaluate the content of your work rather than the specific formatting choices you make. However, it is important that you communicate your ideas and findings clearly and professionally.

Please make sure to appropriately acknowledge any research papers, datasets, software tools (e.g., Neuroglancer and neuPrint), figures, images, or other resources that you use in your report. Giving credit to the work of others is an important part of scientific research and allows readers to trace the sources of information, ideas, and methods used in your project.

If you are unfamiliar with academic referencing, we recommend reviewing the following guide:

Newcastle University Academic Skills Kit: Referencing


https://​www​.ncl​.ac​.uk​/academic​-skills​-kit​/good​-academic​-practice​/referencing/

In brief, referencing means acknowledging the sources of information that you have used in your work.

This is generally a two-step process:

When referring to information, ideas, methods, datasets, or findings from another source, include a citation within the text of your report.

For example:

The complete adult Drosophila brain connectome was recently reconstructed using electron microscopy data (Scheffer et al., 2020).

In this example, (Scheffer et al., 2020) is an in-text citation. It identifies the authors and publication year of the source from which the information originated. You insert the citation within the sentence to indicate the source of the information. In this case, the citation refers to the study by Scheffer and colleagues in 2020 (https://doi.org/10.7554/eLife.57443), and it is formatted in APA style as (Scheffer et al., 2020).

There are many citation styles, including APA, Harvard, MLA, and Vancouver. You are welcome to use any citation style, provided that you remain consistent throughout your report.

At the end of your report, include a References section containing the full bibliographic information for every source cited in the text. For example, the full APA-style reference would be:

Example APA Reference

Scheffer, L. K., Xu, C. S., Januszewski, M., Lu, Z., Takemura, S. Y., Hayworth, K. J., Huang, G. B., Shinomiya, K., Maitin-Shepard, J., Berg, S., Clements, J., Hubbard, P., Katz, W. T., Umayam, L. A., Zhao, T., Ackerman, D., Blakely, T., Bogovic, J., Dolafi, T., ... Plaza, S. M. (2020). A connectome and analysis of the adult Drosophila central brain. eLife, 9, e57443. https://doi.org/10.7554/eLife.57443

As a general rule, you should provide references for:

Research papers and review articles

Datasets

Software tools and platforms (e.g., Neuroglancer, neuPrint)

Figures, images, and visualizations that you did not create yourself

Books, websites, and online resources

Methods, concepts, or ideas that originate from another source

When in doubt, it is usually better to provide a citation than to omit one.

Proper referencing is a fundamental part of scientific integrity and helps ensure that credit is given to the researchers and communities whose work supports your own.
If you use neuPrint or Neuroglancer in your analyses, visualizations, or report, we encourage you to cite the corresponding resources.

APA Style Reference

Plaza, S. M., Clements, J., Dolafi, T., Umayam, L., Neubarth, N. N., Scheffer, L. K., & Berg, S. (2022). neuPrint: An open access tool for EM connectomics. Frontiers in Neuroinformatics, 16, 896292. https://doi.org/10.3389/fninf.2022.896292

APA Style Reference

Maitin-Shepard, J. (2020). Neuroglancer [Computer software]. 

https://​github​.com​/google​/neuroglancer

Example In-Text Citation

neuPrint has become a widely used platform for exploring connectomics datasets (Plaza et al., 2022). Similarly, Neuroglancer provides an interactive environment for visualizing large-scale volumetric neuroscience data (Maitin-Shepard, 2020).

We recognize that there are multiple ways to cite software tools. The examples above are provided as recommended citations for participants who use neuPrint or Neuroglancer in their projects.

records.content:
For thousands of years, humanity has wrestled with one of the deepest questions in science and philosophy:

How does the brain give rise to the mind?

How do billions of tiny cells generate our thoughts, memories, emotions, perceptions, creativity, and consciousness? How does the physical wiring of the brain produce the rich inner world that allows us to learn, dream, communicate, and experience reality?

From the philosophers of ancient Greece to modern neuroscientists, the relationship between the brain and the mind has remained one of the greatest mysteries in human history.

Today, however, we are living through an extraordinary scientific revolution.

records.content:
In this competition, students will explore the brain from two complementary perspectives.

At the microscopic scale, you will investigate one of the most remarkable scientific achievements of our time: the complete synapse-resolution connectome of the adult Drosophila melanogaster (fruit fly) brain. This connectome contains over 160,000 neurons and approximately 170 million synaptic connections, making it the largest complete wiring diagram of an adult animal brain ever reconstructed. Despite its tiny size, the fruit fly is capable of sophisticated behaviors including sensory perception, navigation, learning, memory, and decision-making, making it one of the most powerful model organisms in neuroscience.

Using cutting-edge visualization and analysis tools developed by leading researchers in the field, you will be able to navigate beautiful three-dimensional neurons, trace neural pathways, investigate connectivity patterns, and ask your own research questions about how information flows through biological circuits. You will be using the dataset such as the one shown in the video below!

At the macroscopic scale, you will explore the human functional connectome—the dynamic networks formed when different regions of the brain activate together. Using real large-scale neuroimaging data from over 200 participants, alongside extensive behavioral and cognitive measurements, you will investigate how patterns of brain connectivity relate to individual differences in cognition, behavior, and mental function. The video below gives a nice introduction to human structural and functional connectome!

Together, these two perspectives provide a unique opportunity to study the brain across scales: from individual synapses to whole-brain networks, from structural wiring to dynamic activity, and from neurons to behavior.

records.content:
Connectome2026 is organized in partnership with researchers working at the forefront of connectomics, computational neuroscience, and neuroimaging.

The competition is chaired by graduate researchers affiliated with the University of Oxford and the University of Toronto, and is hosted in partnership with faculty members whose research has helped advance our understanding of neural circuits, cognition, and brain connectivity, including Prof. Eyal Gruntman, Prof. Ina Anreiter, Prof. Morten Kringelbach, and Prof. Steve Joordens.

Through this competition, we hope to share not only the excitement of scientific discovery, but also the tools, techniques, and ways of thinking used by researchers tackling some of neuroscience’s most important questions.

Students will also have the opportunity to attend guest lectures from researchers at world-leading institutions. Previous competitions have featured pioneers in artificial intelligence, connectomics, and Drosophila neuroscience, offering participants a rare chance to learn directly from scientists who have helped shape these rapidly advancing fields.

Most importantly, you do not need prior experience in neuroscience or programming to participate.

We have carefully designed the competition to be accessible to students from diverse backgrounds. Whether you are completely new to neuroscience, have never written a line of code, or already have research experience, our goal is to provide the guidance, resources, and support necessary for you to engage with real scientific data and meaningful research questions.

We deeply value curiosity, persistence, and a willingness to learn. Through this experience, you will gain exposure to modern neuroscience, data science, programming, scientific communication, and research methodology—skills that are valuable not only in academia, but across medicine, technology, engineering, business, and many other fields.

We hope that Connectome2026 serves not only as a competition, but as a launchpad for future scientists, innovators, and problem-solvers.
